newsitem.title: USA: Slovenia, Romania court U.S. support for NATO.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia, Romania court U.S. support for NATO.

text.p: They came to Washington this week courting U.S. support for their bid to enter the NATO military alliance, but Slovenian and Romanian officials were told no decisions have been made.

Seeking to overcome their image as long-shot candidates, both East European countries sent senior officials to the American capital with glossy press kits and lists of reasons why they should be part of the NATO expansion wave this year.

But the Clinton administration told both it has not yet decided which former eastern bloc countries to back when the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation meets in Madrid in July to announce expansion plans, a senior U.S. official said.

"We are not winking or nodding or slipping them little love notes," the official said on Tuesday after the administration opened its doors to Romanian Foreign Minister Adrian Severin and Slovenian Deputy Foreign Minister Ivo Vajgl.
"Both countries are very impressive. But we have not made our decisions yet and we are not whispering in anybody's ear," the official said.
Of 12 former eastern bloc countries to apply, Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are widely considered the front-runners to be invited to apply for membership.

U.S. officials were taking their first real look at Romania's candidacy since a reformist government took over from ex-communists last year. "They certainly win the award for the most improved central-east European country in the past year. But it's still new," the senior official said.
While no serious reservations have been raised about Slovenia's ability to meet the criteria for joining, it lacks a major NATO ally strongly pushing its case.
All the same, Severin and Vajgl seemed upbeat.

"We do expect the United States to come forward and support Slovenia explicitly," Vajgl told a news conference on Tuesday morning, after meetings at the State and Defence departments and just before he visited the White House.
He said support for Slovenia's candidacy was especially strong in the Pentagon, and that Slovenia also has supporters in the U.S. Senate, which must approve any NATO expansion.
Severin was more cautious, but hopeful all the same, in his comments to reporters on Tuesday afternoon, after two days of meetings that included Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.
The Americans said they "would consider it (Romania's candidacy) very seriously ... There was a clear acceptance of the fact that Romania is a very serious candidate," he said.
Severin said he told U.S. officials that the long-run costs of leaving Romania out of NATO could be higher for the United States than the costs of taking it in.

For example, he said a Romania in NATO could send troops to Bosnia to replace American ones involved in peace-keeping duties there once the United States pulls them out. "Romania could do this. We are there, it is less costly, and we are very well respected there," he said.

Severin said Romania had "energetic, clear and open support" for its candidacy from the southern flank of NATO -- including Italy, Spain, France and Portugal, adding that "we have a clear committment for support from Canada."
He said there was more caution in Germany and Britain.

Vajgl said Slovenia had met all the criteria NATO has set for new members, including a stable market economy, democracy and recognition of human rights, and said the small former Yugoslavian state would not be a financial burden for NATO.
U.S. officials repeatedly have stated that countries not invited to join the alliance this year would be eligible later. But Vajgl said Slovenia did not want to wait.
"It would be a fate we don't like and don't deserve, that Slovenia would be put into a waiting room just to have a credible process of a second expansion of NATO," he said.
